source_text: Secundum istam quam dixi miseram conpassionem laudantur illi et a rege Dauid benedicuntur, qui Saulis et Ionathae ossibus aridis sepulturae misericordiam praestiterunt. quae tandem misericordia praestatur nihil sentientibus: an forte reuocandum est in opinionem, quod infernum fluuium insepulti non poterant transmeare? absit hoc a fide christiana: alioquin pessime actum est cum tanta martyrum multitudine, quorum non potuerunt corpora sepeliri, et fallaciter eis ueritas dixit: nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt et postea non habent quid faciant, si eis tanta mala facere potuerunt, quibus inpedirentur ad loca exoptata transire. sed quia hoc sine ulla dubitatione falsissimum est nec aliquid obest fidelibus negata eorum corporibus sepultura nec aliquid, si exhibeatur infidelibus, prodest, cur ergo illi, qui Saulem et eius filium sepelierunt, misericordiam fecisse dicuntur et ob hoc a rege pio benedicuntur, nisi quia bene afficiuntur corda miserantium, quando ea dolent in mortuorum corporibus alienis, quae illo affectu, quo nemo umquam carnem suam odio habet, nolunt fieri post mortem suam corporibus suis, et quod sibi exhiberi uolunt, quando sensuri non sunt, aliis non sentientibus curant exhibere, dum ipsi sentiunt?
thought_title: Why burying Saul and Jonathan was mercy, though the dead feel nothing
orientation: Augustine is answering an objection: if burial does not help the dead, why were the men who buried Saul and Jonathan praised and blessed for showing mercy?
pass_a_gloss: According to this wretched compassion which I have described, those men are praised and are blessed by King David, who showed the mercy of burial to the dry bones of Saul and Jonathan. What mercy, after all, is shown to those who feel nothing? Or perhaps we must return to the belief that those who were unburied could not cross the river of the underworld? Far be this from the Christian faith. Otherwise it went very badly with so great a multitude of martyrs, whose bodies could not be buried, and the truth spoke falsely to them when it said: do not fear those who kill the body and afterwards have nothing more that they can do, if those men could do such great evils to them, by which they would be hindered from crossing over to the places they longed for. But because this is most false without any doubt, and denial of burial to their bodies harms the faithful not at all, and if burial is provided to the unfaithful it benefits them not at all, why then are those who buried Saul and his son said to have shown mercy, and for this reason are blessed by the pious king, except because the hearts of those who show pity are well disposed, when they grieve over those things in the bodies of the dead belonging to others, which, by that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, they do not wish to happen to their own bodies after their death, and what they wish to be shown to themselves, when they will not be able to feel it, they take care to show to others who do not feel it, while they themselves do feel?

choices.why: Keeps the negative force of 'miseram' and the compound sense of shared feeling in 'conpassionem'; Augustine is describing the living's grief for the dead as a pitiable shared suffering.
Literal rendering of the adjective 'aridis'; the dryness emphasizes that the bones were long dead and without flesh, so the mercy was shown to remains that could feel nothing.
Keeps the genitive construction and the glossary term 'burial' for 'sepultura'; the mercy consists in providing burial.
Uses the glossary term 'underworld' for 'infernum' and keeps the pagan poetic image of a river that the unburied cannot cross; Augustine is rejecting this belief.

choices.english: far be this from the Christian faith
choices.why: Standard literal rendering of the optative formula 'absit'; preserves the strong rejection.

choices.english: the hearts of those who show pity are well disposed
choices.why: Keeps the passive of 'afficio' and the present participle 'miserantium' as 'those who show pity'; the point is that the disposition of the living heart is what is praised, not any benefit to the dead.
rejected: the hearts of the pitying are well affected
the hearts of those who pity are moved well

bible_refs.note: laudantur illi et a rege Dauid benedicuntur, qui Saulis et Ionathae ossibus aridis sepulturae misericordiam praestiterunt
nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt et postea non habent quid faciant

pass_b_english: It is by this wretched compassion I have described that those men are praised and blessed by King David who showed the mercy of burial to the dry bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:12-14). But what mercy is being shown to those who feel nothing? Are we to drag back the belief that the unburied could not cross the river of the underworld? Far be this from the Christian faith. Otherwise things went very badly for that great crowd of martyrs whose bodies could not be buried, and the Truth spoke falsely to them when he said: Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do (Matthew 10:28)—if those killers could do such great evils to them as to block their way to the places they longed to reach. But since this is beyond any doubt utterly false, and it does no harm to the faithful if burial is denied to their bodies, nor does it benefit the unfaithful if it is given to them, why then are those who buried Saul and his son said to have shown mercy, and blessed for it by a pious king? Is it not because the hearts of those who show pity are well disposed when they grieve over the bodies of the dead—bodies not their own—for things which, by that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, they do not wish to happen to their own bodies after death? And what they wish to be done for themselves when they will feel nothing, they take care to do for others who feel nothing, while they themselves do feel.

problems.source_quote: qui Saulis et Ionathae ossibus aridis sepulturae misericordiam praestiterunt
problems.why: The burial of Saul and Jonathan's bones is narrated in 2 Samuel 21:12-14, not 2 Samuel 2:5.

fixed: Changed scripture citation from 2 Samuel 2:5 to 2 Samuel 21:12-14, which is where the burial of Saul and Jonathan's bones is narrated.

last_rejected.source_quote: Saulis et Ionathae ossibus aridis sepulturae misericordiam praestiterunt
last_rejected.why: Augustine cites David's burial of Saul and Jonathan's bones, but 2 Samuel 21:12-14 describes David burying Saul and Jonathan's bones retrieved from Jabesh-gilead, not the original burial. The burial itself is in 1 Samuel 31:13 / 1 Chronicles 10:12. The reference should likely be to 1 Samuel 31 or 2 Samuel 21 for the bones.
last_rejected.ruling: 2 Samuel 21:12-14 correctly describes David burying Saul and Jonathan's bones; reference is accurate.

last_rejected.why: The final clause "dum ipsi sentiunt" (while they themselves feel/are aware) is present but its force is weakened; however, the English does render it. Re-checking: actually present. Withdrawing—no, the English has it. Re-reading: the English "while they themselves do feel" captures "dum ipsi sentiunt". Not an omission.
last_rejected.ruling: Checker withdrew; 'dum ipsi sentiunt' is rendered as 'while they themselves do feel.'
